CHAPTER 3.2 · LEARNING AREA 3 · FEBRUARY · MARCH

Symmetry and reflection

A butterfly, a church window, a road sign, a playing card: you discover symmetry everywhere. You learn to recognise figures with line symmetry and point symmetry, tell translation, rotation and reflection apart and construct mirror images accurately with the set square.

10 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • discover symmetry in patterns, buildings, signs and in nature
  • tell line symmetry and point symmetry apart and draw in lines of symmetry
  • recognise whether a figure has been translated, rotated or reflected
  • reflect figures in a line and describe the drawing steps
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How do the opposite sides of a rectangle lie?

Opposite sides are parallel.

Through how many degrees do you have to rotate a figure so that it is upside down?

half a turn

What is the x-coordinate of the point that lies exactly halfway between (4, 2) and (10, 2)?

$(4 + 10) \div 2$

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
BLOT PICTURE

Drip some paint onto a sheet of paper, fold it in the middle and press firmly. Open it again.

  • What do you notice about the picture? Where is the fold line?
  • Hold a pocket mirror on the fold line. What do you see?
→ Unit 1
UPSIDE DOWN

Write down the capital letters A to Z and turn the sheet round by half a turn.

  • Which letters look exactly the same afterwards? Which have a mirror line?
→ Unit 1
HOW DID IT GET THERE?

Put a template (for example a foot made of card) on a sheet of paper and draw round it. Then move it and draw round it again.

  • The others have to guess: slid, turned or flipped over?
→ Unit 2
UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Line symmetry and point symmetry

In the blot picture both halves are mirror images of each other. The fold line is the line of symmetry. The letters H, I, N, O, S, X and Z look exactly the same after half a turn. H, I, O and X also have mirror lines, N, S and Z do not.

KEY POINT · SYMMETRY

A figure has line symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that both halves lie exactly on top of each other. The line is called the line of symmetry. A figure can have several lines of symmetry.

A figure has point symmetry if it lands exactly on itself after a half turn (180°) about a point. The point is called the centre of symmetry.

Many lines: A square has 4 lines of symmetry, an equilateral triangle 3, a circle infinitely many.

Playing cards such as the queen of spades are usually printed with point symmetry. That way they look right whichever way round you hold them.

INTERACTIVE · PATTERN WORKSHOP
EXAMPLE 1 · COUNTING LINES

How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have that is not a square?

The lines go through the midpoints of opposite sides. The diagonals are not lines of symmetry: if you fold along them, corners stick out.

2 lines of symmetry, and it also has point symmetry.

EXAMPLE 2 · DIGITS

Which of the digits 0 to 9 (written as on a digital clock) have point symmetry?

After half a turn 0, 1, 2, 5 and 8 look exactly the same. 6 becomes 9 and vice versa.

0, 1, 2, 5, 8

EXERCISES

Copy the figures and draw in all the lines of symmetry: square, equilateral triangle, rhombus (not a square), circle, parallelogram (not a rectangle).

Square 4, equilateral triangle 3, rhombus 2 (the diagonals), circle infinitely many, parallelogram none (but it has point symmetry).

Which words have a vertical line of symmetry if you write them in capital letters one below the other? OTTO, ANNA, TOM, WOW, MUM

Written one below the other: OTTO, TOM, WOW and MUM, because each of their letters has a vertical line of symmetry. In ANNA the N spoils it.

Look around you for two examples each of things with line symmetry and with point symmetry. Photograph them or draw them.

For example line symmetry: a leaf, a face, the “Give way” sign. Point symmetry: a propeller with two blades, the queen of spades, a football pitch with its lines.

A figure has two lines of symmetry that are perpendicular to each other. Explain why it then also has point symmetry. Try it in the pattern workshop with “two lines”.

First reflect in one line, then in the other: together that gives a half turn about the point of intersection. Because both reflections map the figure onto itself, so does the rotation.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

two through the midpoints of the sides, two diagonals

Which letter has point symmetry but not line symmetry?

S lands on itself after half a turn but has no line of symmetry.

Through what angle do you rotate for point symmetry?

half a turn

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Translation, rotation, reflection

If the card foot was turned over, a left foot has become a right foot: that was a reflection. If all the toes still point in the same direction, it was only slid.

With all three transformations the figure stays the same size and the same shape. What changes is its position. The new figure is called the image, its points $A'$, $B'$, … (read “A dash”).

KEY POINT · THREE TRANSFORMATIONS

Translation: All points move the same distance in the same direction, described by an arrow. All line segments stay parallel to how they were before.

Rotation: All points turn about the same point Z through the same angle. Every point stays the same distance from Z.

Reflection: The figure is flipped over in a line. The orientation changes: “anticlockwise” becomes “clockwise”.

How to tell: If the image is flipped over, it was a reflection. If it is not flipped over and all sides point in the old direction, it was a translation. Otherwise a rotation.

INTERACTIVE · TRANSFORMATIONS AND PUZZLES
EXAMPLE 3 · TRANSLATION

The triangle A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 3) is translated 5 to the right and 2 up. Give the image points.

Add 5 to every x-coordinate and 2 to every y-coordinate.

A′(6, 3), B′(9, 3), C′(6, 5)

EXAMPLE 4 · WHICH TRANSFORMATION?

The letter F becomes an upside-down F that you can read quite normally if you turn the sheet. Which transformation was it?

The F is not flipped over, otherwise it would be a mirror F.

a rotation through 180°

EXERCISES

Translate the quadrilateral A(0, 0), B(3, 0), C(3, 2), D(1, 3) 4 to the right and 1 up. Give the coordinates of the image points.

A′(4, 1), B′(7, 1), C′(7, 3), D′(5, 4)

Solve five puzzles in the widget. Write down how you recognised the transformation each time.

Flipped over: reflection. Only moved, same direction: translation. Tilted but not flipped over: rotation.

Which transformation does a) a lift   b) a horse on the merry-go-round   c) your mirror image in the bathroom   d) a drawer being pulled out make?

a) translation   b) rotation about the centre of the merry-go-round   c) reflection   d) translation

Reflect a figure twice in succession in two parallel lines that are 3 units apart. Which single transformation would have the same result? Try it on squared paper.

A translation by 6 units perpendicular to the lines, so twice as far as the distance between the lines.

TEST YOURSELF!

B(4, 1) is translated 5 to the right and 2 up. What is the x-coordinate of B′?

$4 + 5$

With which transformation does the orientation change?

Only the reflection flips over.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Reflecting in a line

With the pocket mirror on the fold line the blot picture looks complete again. Every point seems to lie just as far behind the mirror as it lies in front of it.

KEY POINT · REFLECTING WITH THE SET SQUARE
  1. Put the middle line of the set square on the mirror line $s$ and slide it until its edge goes through the point $P$.
  2. Draw the perpendicular to $s$ through $P$.
  3. Measure the distance from $P$ to the mirror line and mark it off again on the other side. That is $P'$.
  4. Do the same with all the vertices and join the image points.

Original and image are the same size: corresponding sides are equal in length, corresponding angles are equal. Points on the mirror line stay where they are.

On squared paper it works without a set square for horizontal or vertical mirror lines: count the squares to the mirror line and go the same number further on the other side.

In the coordinate system with the mirror line $x = 7$: $P(5, 3)$ becomes $P'(9, 3)$, because 5 lies 2 to the left of 7 and 9 lies 2 to the right of it.

INTERACTIVE · REFLECTION IN A LINE
EXAMPLE 5 · VERTICAL MIRROR LINE

Reflect A(2, 1), B(5, 1), C(5, 3) in the line $x = 7$.

Distances to the mirror line: A 5, B 2, C 2. On the other side: $7 + 5 = 12$, $7 + 2 = 9$.

A′(12, 1), B′(9, 1), C′(9, 3)

EXAMPLE 6 · SLANTING MIRROR LINE

Where does the mirror image of P(4, 1) lie in the slanting mirror line through (0, 0) and (5, 5)?

With this mirror line the x- and y-coordinates swap places. Check with the set square: the line joining P and P′ is perpendicular to the mirror line.

P′(1, 4)

EXERCISES

Reflect the triangle A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(2, 5) in the line $x = 6$. Draw it and give the coordinates of the image points.

A′(11, 2), B′(8, 2), C′(10, 5)

Reflect the same triangle in the line $y = 6$.

A′(1, 10), B′(4, 10), C′(2, 7)

Describe in full sentences how you reflect a point P in a slanting line $s$. A partner draws only from your description.

See the key point box: draw the perpendicular to $s$ through P, measure the distance, mark off the same distance on the other side.

P(3, 2) and its mirror image P′(7, 6) are given. Where is the mirror line? Draw it.

The mirror line goes through the midpoint of the line segment $\overline{PP'}$ and is perpendicular to it.

Midpoint M(5, 4). The line segment $\overline{PP'}$ rises 4 for every 4 to the right; the mirror line is perpendicular to it: it goes through M and, for example, (6, 3) and (4, 5).

TEST YOURSELF!

P(5, 3) is reflected in $x = 7$. What is the x-coordinate of P′?

2 to the left of 7, so 2 to the right of it

A(1, 2) is reflected in $y = 6$. What is the y-coordinate of A′?

4 below the mirror line, so 4 above it

How does the line joining P and P′ lie in relation to the mirror line?

always perpendicular

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Complete the figure to make a figure with line symmetry with the mirror line $x = 5$: A(2, 1), B(5, 1), C(5, 4), D(3, 4).

The mirror images of A and D are A′(8, 1) and D′(7, 4). B and C lie on the mirror line. The whole figure: A, A′, D′, D.

Connecting with chapter 3.1: A line forms an angle of 35° with the mirror line. What angle does its mirror image form with the mirror line? What angle do the line and its mirror image form with each other?

The mirror image also forms 35° with the mirror line (angles stay the same), on the other side. Together they form 70° (or the adjacent angle 110°).

Design a pattern with two lines of symmetry in the pattern workshop. How many squares do you have to click yourself so that 24 squares are coloured at the end?

Every square produces three more. You need $24 \div 4 = 6$ clicks if none of them lies on a line of symmetry.

EXCURSIONART

Escher and the tiles of the Alhambra

The Alhambra in Granada in Spain is a Moorish palace from the 13th and 14th centuries. Its walls are covered with tile patterns that repeat without gaps, reflected, rotated and translated.

The Dutch artist M. C. Escher visited the Alhambra for the first time in 1922 and copied the patterns. In 1936 he came back with his wife Jetta and spent days copying the tiles. After that the patterns never let go of him. He invented his own tessellations in which fish, birds, lizards and horsemen instead of stars and polygons fill the plane without gaps. Behind each of these pictures is exactly what you have learnt in this chapter: translations, rotations and reflections.

Try it yourself: cut a piece out of one side of a square and stick it back on the opposite side. With this shape you can fill a sheet without gaps.

Sources: D. Schattschneider: Visions of Symmetry. Notebooks, Periodic Drawings, and Related Work of M. C. Escher. W. H. Freeman, New York 1990. Escher in Het Paleis, The Hague.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

LINE SYMMETRY

Fold along the line of symmetry: both halves lie on top of each other

square: 4 lines

POINT SYMMETRY

half turn (180°) about the centre of symmetry

S, N, Z, parallelogram

TRANSFORMATIONS

Translation, rotation, reflection: size and shape stay the same, only the reflection flips over.

A(1, 1) → A′(6, 3)

REFLECTION IN A LINE

Perpendicular to the mirror line, same distance on the other side

in $x = 7$: P(5, 3) → P′(9, 3)
